name: glass
description: Glass: VU meters, spectrum, turntables and reels on the player's display
author: foonerd; audio path from PeppyMeter Screensaver by 2aCD (original) and Just a Nerd

volumio_info.details: Glass draws VU meters, spectrum analysers, turntables and tape decks on the player's display from PeppyMeter themes. It is a native display, one small binary, with no Python and no browser in the path. Glass replaces PeppyMeter Screensaver: only one of the two may be enabled.
volumio_info.changelog: 0.7.75 A Face or a display that attaches mid-track starts at the right position. 0.7.74 The screen without X: a Screen panel on the System tab with the driver (KMS/DRM among them) and the rotation. 0.7.73 The Catalog reads the collection under its new name, glass_templates. 0.7.72 A cut theme's disc and reels turn about the right point, and its screen picture sits where the theme does. 0.7.71 Package shows its progress meter by meter, and the card says when a job runs. 0.7.70 Tailor and Package on the Manager's Themes tab. 0.7.69 A theme named by its whole path keeps its size, so a package shows the theme whole. 0.7.68 The package: glass --package writes a theme with a preview as a catalogue zip. 0.7.67 The cutter: glass --tailor writes a copy of a theme at another size. 0.7.66 The old plugin's themes are copied once, not at every upgrade; a button's pictures one per state; the onsets and one-bit audio reach the ring and the wire; the volume number in its own font; a single layout draws a stereo bank's mean; a track's pictures only from the playing track's folder. 0.7.50 The sample rate beside the format icon as one line; pictures that cover their box. 0.7.49 The analyser draws forty times cheaper; its level range fits the bank; the volume as a number beside its gauge. 0.7.48 The analyser: spectrum sections drawn as anti-aliased bars from palettes, with peaks, layouts, LEDs, mirror and reflection, on audioMotion's keys; on Anymote the first tap takes the screen. 0.7.43 The Status tab as a system sheet, with Copy as text and addresses revealed on request; the face keeps the player's state across a refresh. 0.7.42 The face takes a finger: taps and drags on the controls act on the player; Anymote, any remote, a remote from anywhere: the face on a page of its own for any browser. 0.7.41 The Face tab: the player's meters live in any browser, drawn by the display's own engine compiled for the browser. 0.7.40 Controls grow to a finger's size and the bars drag. 0.7.39 Interactive controls: a theme's indicators and buttons act on a tap; a setting says as the theme says, on, or off. 0.7.38 Car Dash by the sun, from the time zone's place or your own. 0.7.37 Car Dash: a day theme and a night theme by the clock, on the Themes tab. 0.7.36 Remotes: Escape leaves full screen and keeps showing, F returns, Q quits; the page has the buttons. 0.7.35 The remote's page says when the remote has stopped. 0.7.34 The Linux display archives are small again. 0.7.33 Remotes: the status screen in a proper face; Android names its real address. 0.7.32 Remotes: configuration export and import, the log level and a spectrum decay on the page. 0.7.31 Remotes: themes from a folder on the remote's own machine, and the screen to open on. 0.7.30 A fuller Status tab: theme folders, fonts, network share, fanart, performance. 0.7.29 Themes taken over from PeppyMeter Screensaver are copied into Glass's own folder, the old one left as it was. 0.7.28 Text set in the built-in fonts sits and sizes as under PeppyMeter. 0.7.27 Fonts of your own: upload a font and set each text style in it. 0.7.26 Themes can be edited over the network share again. 0.7.25 Text in every script again: the PeppyFont set is back, with a glyph-by-glyph fallback. 0.7.24 Artist fanart shows on remotes. 0.7.23 The first signed release. 0.7.22 The Windows binary is signed. 0.7.21 The first release with the Android app. 0.7.20 Glass runs as a remote display on Android. 0.7.19 On Windows no console window opens behind the display, and the executable carries an icon. 0.7.18 The remote opens its window on Windows. 0.7.17 A remote's page says when it cannot read the remote; a switch on the Performance panel turns that off. 0.7.12 glass --dev opens a movable window at the theme's exact size for reviewing. 0.7.11 A System tab in the manager for releases, the performance profile and logging. 0.7.10 Logging with levels and targets, and performance profiles, on the Status tab; the display's lines reach the journal as they are written; an upgrade waits for the plugin registry before it restarts. 0.7.9 A remote shows the pictures a theme takes from the playing track's folder. 0.7.8 One line installs Glass on a player: get-glass.sh, fetched with curl. 0.7.7 A remote that follows the player shows the meter the player shows. 0.7.6 A remote keeps moving across a track change: the frames daemon numbers its datagrams itself and the remote trusts the player's stamps. 0.7.5 A remote that follows the player follows its whole configuration and hears it on every connection; the wiki rewritten around a Quick Start. 0.7.4 A remote's needles and bars move as the player's own do: the frames daemon sends the frames in each hop, and the remote times its decay by the player's stamps. 0.7.3 A remote display is set up on a page of its own: its players, a theme followed or kept as its own, its window, frame rate and gain, applied while it runs; the Remotes tab links to each remote's page. 0.7.2 The status tab says whether remote displays are served, on which ports, and how many receive frames. 0.7.1 Remote displays are served only when the manager's Remotes tab says so, with the ports set there; a player with no screen of its own serves remotes without opening a window. 0.7.0 Remote displays: Glass on another machine shows this player's meters with its theme, fonts and icons; the plugin sends the frames, serves the channel over TCP, announces the player, and lists the remotes in the manager. 0.6.11 The measured line no longer calls a playing source unmeasured when the ring's stamp lands a hair ahead of the manager's clock. 0.6.10 The status tab says whether what plays is measured, from the tap's rings, so a source playing below the tap is seen at a glance. 0.6.9 Soloist Connect plays again with Glass running: it stays on the player's own device, where the tap measures it, and Glass nudges it after every rewrite of the ALSA file so a device sampled mid-start is corrected. 0.6.8 Soloist Connect meters again after a backend start: Glass tells Soloist its metering is on after every rewrite of the ALSA file, so Soloist opens the tap (plug:spotify) rather than a device read from a half-written file. 0.6.7 The settings backups an upgrade writes on its own are kept to the newest five; named backups are never touched. 0.6.6 'Open the manager here' opens it in this window, inside Volumio's page, instead of a new tab; the manager's inputs take the kiosk's on-screen keyboard. 0.6.5 The settings page sets the manager's port (the manager moves at once, and says when the port is taken) and its address for players where .local names do not resolve. 0.6.4 A settings backup downloads as a zip and a zip uploads as a backup, so settings move from one player to another. 0.6.3 The restart after an upgrade is one systemd restart job, so the backend comes back on its own. 0.6.2 The manager looks for a new release a minute after start and once a day, and says so in its header. 0.6.1 Glass upgrades itself from the manager: the latest release is checked on GitHub, its zip downloaded and verified against the release digest, the settings backed up and the installed plugin kept for going back, then the player's plugin manager replaces the plugin and the backend restarts. 0.6.0 The Glass Manager: a web application the plugin serves on its own port for everything that manages the display. Installed themes with previews the display draws itself, the theme catalog with checksum-verified installs and updates, theme uploads, the meter rotation, the artist fanart settings, settings backups and a status page. The settings page keeps what operates the display and opens the manager.
